summary: Specifies the Versatile Message Transaction Protocol (VMTP), a transport protocol designed for the request-and-response style of communication used by remote procedure calls. It offers features such as security, real-time use, streaming, multicast and idempotency, and can be trimmed down for simple clients and servers. It was experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: The Versatile Message Transaction Protocol (VMTP) carries requests and responses, especially for remote procedure calls. It includes acknowledgments and retransmissions for reliability, while allowing systems to omit features they do not need.

subtitle: A transport protocol built around reliable request-and-response transactions.

tldr.problem: Remote procedure calls need a transport that can deliver requests and responses reliably without a separate connection setup for every exchange.
tldr.mechanism: VMTP identifies transactions, acknowledges messages, retransmits missing packets, and supports streaming, multicast, security, and simplified implementations.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies an Experimental transport protocol and describes optional features that implementations can specialize for their needs.

today: RFC 1045 is Experimental. It specifies the VMTP protocol and describes its client, server, packet, and management operations.

sections.title: Communication as a Transaction
sections.content:
VMTP treats communication as a transaction: a client sends a request to a server, the server processes it, and the server sends a response. There is no separate transport-level operation to establish or close a client-server association for each transaction.

A request may target one server or a group. A group transaction can produce responses from multiple servers, and the protocol can also support asynchronous and nested requests.
sections.plainLanguage: A client asks for work in a request, and a server answers with a response. VMTP does not require a separate connection setup before each request.

sections.title: Stable Identities for Communication Endpoints
sections.content:
VMTP communicates with entities identified by entity identifiers, rather than relying only on the current network address of a host. An entity can move between hosts or use a host with multiple addresses while retaining its logical identity.

The RFC distinguishes an entity, the process acting for it, and the security principal associated with it. Entity domains define where identifiers are unique and stable, and can separate different administrative or security namespaces.
sections.plainLanguage: An entity identifier names the communication endpoint even if its host address changes. A domain sets the scope in which those identifiers are managed.

sections.title: Acknowledgments and Retransmission
sections.content:
VMTP gives each transaction an identifier so a server can recognize duplicate requests. It uses packet checksums, positive acknowledgments, timeouts, and retransmissions to recover when packets are lost on an unreliable datagram network.

Messages can span multiple packets, and the receiver can request retransmission of selected portions. VMTP also uses a rate-control mechanism that adjusts gaps between packets when loss indicates that a receiver or part of the path is being overrun.
sections.plainLanguage: Transaction numbers help the server recognize repeated requests. When packets are missing, the receiver can ask for the missing parts instead of starting the whole message again.

sections.title: Optional Capabilities
sections.content:
VMTP supports optional secure transactions, multicast requests with multiple responses, real-time behavior, forwarded transactions, streaming, and packet groups. A packet group collects packets for sequencing, acknowledgment, selective retransmission, and rate control.

The protocol can be reduced for simple clients and servers that need only a subset of these services. This flexibility is intended to let systems use the mechanisms required by their application without implementing every feature.
sections.plainLanguage: VMTP offers features such as security, multicast, and streaming, but a small implementation can leave out features it does not use. Packet groups organize multi-packet messages for recovery and pacing.

sections.title: Security and Protocol Operation
sections.content:
Secure VMTP can encrypt requests and responses and detect impersonation, replay, and message changes. The RFC warns that non-secure VMTP cannot guarantee its reliability properties when an attacker can modify packets and checksums.

Security is optional, and a separate key-distribution and authentication protocol is needed to provision authenticators and keys. The rest of the RFC specifies packet formats and client and server event processing for the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption and authentication protect VMTP messages when secure mode is used. Without that protection, an attacker who can change packets can undermine the protocol's reliability checks.
